title: The List Contract & ArrayList Internals
summary: Go deep under the hood of Java's most widely used collection. Explore internal backing array resizing, the 1.5x growth factor, fast random access via index math, and insertion shifts.
learningObjectives: Master the List<E> contract: positional access, search, and ListIterator
Dissect the source code internals of java.util.ArrayList (elementData, size, modCount)
Calculate the 1.5x dynamic growth formula: oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)
Understand why get(i) is O(1) constant time and why middle insertions/deletions are O(n)
expectedOutcomes: Clear mental model of how ArrayList manages its internal buffer and when memory reallocation triggers
Ability to write optimized, high-throughput code using ensureCapacity and avoiding unnecessary resizes

activities.title: Practical Context: Dynamic Array Resizing and Amortized Constant Time

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Dynamic Array Resizing and Amortized Constant Time
analogy.story:
In computer science, `ArrayList` is the most widely utilized data structure in the Java language.

While it appears to grow infinitely, under the hood it is powered by a standard contiguous Java array that resizes dynamically.

Understanding how `ArrayList` manages its internal capacity allows software engineers to prevent memory waste and allocation spikes.
analogy.keyTakeaway: ArrayList maintains an internal Object[] buffer. Capacity is the physical buffer size; size is the number of active elements. When full, it grows by 50% (1.5x) and copies elements to the new buffer.

activities.content:
In computer science, `ArrayList` is the most widely utilized data structure in the Java language.

While it appears to grow infinitely, under the hood it is powered by a standard contiguous Java array that resizes dynamically.

Understanding how `ArrayList` manages its internal capacity allows software engineers to prevent memory waste and allocation spikes.

activities.title: ArrayList Architecture: Backing Arrays, 1.5x Resizing, and Time Complexity

keyTakeaways: ArrayList is backed by a package-private buffer: `transient Object[] elementData`
`size` tracks active items; `elementData.length` is the internal capacity
Default initial capacity is 10, lazily allocated upon the first `add()` invocation
`get(index)` is pure pointer math (`baseAddress + index * 4/8 bytes`) → true O(1)

activities.title: Tracing ArrayList Operations & Shifting Overhead
activities.description: Observe how positional insertions shift elements and how pre-sizing eliminates array copy events.
activities.codeSnippet:
ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>(100); // Pre-size
list.add(2, "New Item"); // O(n) right shift
list.get(2); // O(1) instant read

questions.prompt: What is the default initial capacity of an ArrayList when created with 'new ArrayList<>()' in modern Java?
options: 0 initially, then 10 upon the first element addition
questions.explanation: Modern Java uses lazy initialization: new ArrayList<>() points to an empty shared array and allocates the initial capacity of 10 only when add() is first called.

hints.hint: Think about lazy initialization to save memory for unused lists.

questions.prompt: By what factor does an ArrayList increase its capacity when it runs out of space?
questions.explanation: ArrayList expands by ~50% (1.5x) using the bitwise formula: oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1).

questions.prompt: If an ArrayList currently has capacity 20 and becomes full, what will its new capacity be?
Why is 'list.get(index)' an O(1) constant time operation in an ArrayList?
options: It traverses a linked chain of nodes
It performs direct memory pointer arithmetic based on the contiguous backing array
It uses binary search on keys
It caches previous queries in a hash table
questions.explanation: Because the backing array is contiguous in memory, accessing index 'i' is computed directly: address = baseAddress + (i * elementSize), which executes in 1 CPU cycle.

hints.hint: Contiguous memory allows instant offset math.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of inserting an element at index 0 of an ArrayList with N elements?
questions.explanation: Inserting at index 0 requires shifting all N existing elements one position to the right via System.arraycopy, requiring O(N) operations.

hints.hint: All subsequent elements must move forward by one position.

questions.prompt: What marker interface does ArrayList implement to advertise that it supports fast constant-time random access?
questions.explanation: RandomAccess is a marker interface (contains no methods) used by generic algorithms (like Collections.binarySearch) to choose fast indexed loops over iterators.

questions.prompt: What method can be invoked on an ArrayList to trim the capacity of the backing array to the list's current size?
questions.explanation: trimToSize() trims the capacity of the ArrayList instance to be the list's current size, freeing unused memory in the heap.

questions.prompt: Why is the internal backing array 'transient Object[] elementData' declared transient in ArrayList?
options: To prevent serializing unused null slots at the end of the backing array, optimizing network/disk payloads
Transient is required for all arrays in Java
questions.explanation: If elementData has capacity 1000 but size is only 10, default serialization would write 990 useless nulls. By making it transient, ArrayList uses custom writeObject/readObject methods to write only the active 'size' elements.

hints.hint: Consider the serialization of trailing null slots.

questions.prompt: What is the amortized time complexity of appending an element to the end of an ArrayList via 'list.add(e)'?
questions.explanation: While an occasional add() triggers an O(N) resize, the doubling/1.5x strategy spreads this cost across so many subsequent O(1) additions that the average cost per operation is amortized O(1).

hints.hint: Think about amortized average cost across thousands of additions.

questions.prompt: What exception is thrown if you invoke 'list.get(5)' on an ArrayList where 'list.size() == 5'?
questions.explanation: Valid indices for a list of size 5 are 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. Accessing index 5 violates bounds and throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.

hints.hint: 0-based indexing means max index is size - 1.

interviewQA.question: How does ArrayList work internally in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: ArrayList is backed by a dynamic Object[] array. It tracks the element count using a 'size' field. When an element is added and the backing array is full, it dynamically expands by 1.5x using the formula: oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1). Elements are copied to the newly allocated array via Arrays.copyOf (native System.arraycopy).
keyPoints: 1.5x capacity growth factor via bitwise right shift
Amortized O(1) additions; O(1) random reads via index math

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between the size and capacity of an ArrayList?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: 'size' is the actual number of elements currently stored in the list, returned by list.size(). 'capacity' is the total number of slots allocated in the underlying backing array (elementData.length) before resizing is required. Capacity is an internal buffer metric not directly exposed as a public getter.
keyPoints: Capacity = length of backing buffer array

interviewQA.question: Why is elementData declared as 'transient Object[]' in ArrayList?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: If elementData was serialized by default, Java's default serialization mechanism would serialize all unused empty slots (which are null references), wasting significant network bandwidth and storage. Marking it transient allows ArrayList to implement custom writeObject() and readObject() methods that serialize only the valid elements up to 'size'.
keyPoints: Prevents serializing unused null array slots

interviewQA.question: What is the RandomAccess marker interface and why does ArrayList implement it?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: RandomAccess is a marker interface that has no methods. It signals to generic algorithms (such as Collections.binarySearch or shuffle) that the list supports constant-time O(1) indexed access. Algorithms can check 'if (list instanceof RandomAccess)' to use high-speed index-based loops instead of creating Iterator cursor objects.
keyPoints: Used by Collections algorithms to optimize iteration style

interviewQA.question: What is the performance implication of inserting or removing elements at the beginning or middle of an ArrayList?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Inserting or removing at index k requires shifting (size - k) elements to the right or left using System.arraycopy. For index 0, every single element must be copied, making it an O(n) operation. If an application requires frequent head or middle insertions, an ArrayDeque or LinkedList is usually a better fit.
keyPoints: O(n) linear cost for index 0 and middle operations

interviewQA.question: How can you optimize ArrayList performance when inserting a known large number of elements?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: You should use the parameterized constructor 'new ArrayList<>(expectedCapacity)' or invoke 'list.ensureCapacity(expectedCapacity)' before loading data. This pre-allocates the exact required buffer upfront, completely eliminating repeated memory allocations and array copying cycles during growth.
keyPoints: Avoids repeated O(n) reallocation and GC pressure

activities.title: Lesson 3 Mastery Checkpoint
checklist: I understand the difference between size and capacity in ArrayList.
I can calculate the 1.5x expansion formula: oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1).
I know why get(i) is O(1) and why add(i, e) is O(n).
I understand why elementData is marked transient.
I know when and how to use ensureCapacity() to optimize memory throughput.

practiceProblems.title: Capacity Growth Simulator
practiceProblems.description: Calculate and print the capacity growth steps of an ArrayList from 10 elements up to 100 elements.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Write a growth simulation program:

1. In `Main.main()`:
   - Start with an `int capacity = 10;`
   - In a loop, simulate expansions using the exact Java formula: `capacity = capacity + (capacity >> 1)`
   - Continue until capacity exceeds 100.
   - Print each expansion step in the format:
     `Step <stepNum>: Capacity = <capacity>`
   - After the loop, print: `Total Expansions: <stepNum>`
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Step 1: Capacity = 15
Step 2: Capacity = 22
Step 3: Capacity = 33
Step 4: Capacity = 49
Step 5: Capacity = 73
Step 6: Capacity = 109
Total Expansions: 6
practiceProblems.hint: Use capacity = capacity + (capacity >> 1) inside a while (capacity <= 100) loop.
hints: int step = 0; while (capacity <= 100) { step++; capacity = capacity + (capacity >> 1); ... }
Print step and capacity on each iteration.

practiceProblems.title: Pre-Allocation Benchmark Tracker
practiceProblems.description: Compare element insertion into a default-capacity ArrayList versus a pre-sized ArrayList.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Write an insertion benchmark simulator:

1. In `Main.main()`:
   - Create `List<Integer> listDefault = new ArrayList<>();`
   - Insert numbers 1 to 50,000 into `listDefault`.
   - Create `List<Integer> listPresized = new ArrayList<>(50000);`
   - Insert numbers 1 to 50,000 into `listPresized`.
   - Verify both lists have matching sizes and print:
     `Default List Size: <size>`
     `Presized List Size: <size>`
     `Lists Match: <true/false>`
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Default List Size: 50000
Presized List Size: 50000
Lists Match: true
practiceProblems.hint: Verify listDefault.equals(listPresized) to test if both lists hold the same elements in identical order.
hints: Populate using for (int i = 1; i <= 50000; i++)

practiceProblems.title: Middle Shift Cost Calculator
practiceProblems.description: Calculate the exact number of element shifts required when inserting items at specific indices.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Implement a shift calculator function that quantifies the O(n) penalty of positional insertions:

1. Write static method:
   `public static int calculateShifts(int currentSize, int insertIndex)`
   - If `insertIndex < 0 || insertIndex > currentSize`, throw `IndexOutOfBoundsException`.
   - When inserting at `insertIndex`, all elements from `insertIndex` to `currentSize - 1` must shift right by 1 slot.
   - Return the number of elements shifted: `currentSize - insertIndex`.

2. In `Main.main()`:
   - For a list with `currentSize = 10`:
     - Calculate shifts for inserting at index 0 (head)
     - Calculate shifts for inserting at index 5 (middle)
     - Calculate shifts for inserting at index 10 (tail)
   - Print:
     `Head Insert Shifts: <shifts>`
     `Middle Insert Shifts: <shifts>`
     `Tail Insert Shifts: <shifts>`
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Head Insert Shifts: 10
Middle Insert Shifts: 5
Tail Insert Shifts: 0
practiceProblems.hint: Shifts count is currentSize - insertIndex. At index 10 (the tail), 0 elements need to shift!
hints: Head insert at 0 shifts all 10 elements.
Tail append at 10 shifts 0 elements (true O(1)).

practiceProblems.title: Fix Concurrent Modification Off-By-One Deletion
practiceProblems.description: Fix an element-skipping bug when removing elements by index in a forward for-loop.
practiceProblems.hint: Iterate backwards: for (int i = list.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--). Shifting elements to the left only affects higher indices that have already been visited!
hints: Forward removal skips adjacent matching elements.
Backward removal: for (int i = list.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--)

practiceProblems.title: High-Watermark Memory Trimmer
practiceProblems.description: Simulate high burst traffic in an ArrayList and use trimToSize to release unneeded heap buffer.
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a burst buffer processor:

1. In `Main.main()`:
   - Create an `ArrayList<String>` with initial capacity 1000.
   - Add 1,000 temporary batch records: `"RECORD-" + i`.
   - Print: `Peak Size: <list.size()>`
   - Retain only the first 5 records using `list.subList(5, list.size()).clear();`.
   - Call `list.trimToSize()` to shrink the backing array down to 5 slots.
   - Print:
     `Retained Size: <list.size()>`
     `Final Records: <list>`
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Peak Size: 1000
Retained Size: 5
Final Records: [RECORD-0, RECORD-1, RECORD-2, RECORD-3, RECORD-4]
practiceProblems.hint: subList(5, list.size()).clear() clears elements from index 5 onwards. trimToSize() resizes the backing array to size 5.
